title: Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
question: If the universe is vast and full of stars, why isn't every direction in the night sky as bright as the Sun?
summary: A simple argument says an infinite, eternal universe full of stars should have a blazing sky. This exploration traces Olbers' paradox from Kepler to Poe to modern cosmology, showing how the darkness of night reveals the universe's finite age — and how the sky glows after all, in microwaves.
content:
The Most Obvious Question in Astronomy

Why is the night sky dark? It sounds like a child's question, and the child's answer — "because the Sun has set" — seems complete. But in the 1820s the German astronomer Heinrich Olbers sharpened a puzzle that Kepler and Halley had already worried over, and it turns out that explaining the darkness requires nearly all of modern cosmology.

The argument goes like this. Suppose the universe is infinite, eternal, and evenly sprinkled with stars. Draw a thin spherical shell around Earth at some distance. A distant star looks dimmer by the square of its distance, but a shell at that distance contains more stars by exactly the square of its distance. The two effects cancel: every shell contributes the same amount of light. With infinitely many shells, the sky should be infinitely bright — or, since nearer stars block farther ones, every line of sight should end on the surface of a star. The entire sky should blaze like the face of the Sun, day and night.

Wrong Answers That Seem Right

An early proposal was that interstellar dust absorbs the distant light. But absorbed energy heats the dust, which would eventually glow just as brightly as the stars behind it. Absorption only delays the problem. Another idea was that stars are arranged in a hierarchy of clusters with mostly empty space between them; this can work mathematically, but the universe on large scales turns out to be remarkably uniform, so it does not rescue us.

The Real Answer: A Finite Past

The resolution — first glimpsed, remarkably, by Edgar Allan Poe in his 1848 prose poem Eureka — is that the universe has a finite age. Light travels at a finite speed, so we can only see stars whose light has had time to reach us. Looking out, we see a sphere of roughly 13.8 billion years of lookback time, and most lines of sight within it simply do not hit a star before reaching the era before stars existed. The observable universe holds a finite number of stars, and they are far too sparse to cover the sky.

A further point, made precise by Edward Harrison in the twentieth century, is that stars do not live forever. Even if the universe were much older, stars burn out after millions or billions of years; there is simply not enough energy in all the matter of the universe to fill space with starlight at the density of a stellar surface.

Expansion adds a finishing touch. As space stretches, light from distant galaxies is redshifted to longer wavelengths and lower energies, dimming the far universe further. But careful calculation shows that the finite age and finite stellar lifetimes do most of the work; the redshift is a secondary effect.

The Sky Is Not Actually Dark

Here is the twist: in one sense, Olbers was right. Every direction we look does end on a glowing surface — not a star, but the hot plasma that filled the universe about 380,000 years after the Big Bang. That surface was as bright and hot as a star's, around 3,000 kelvin. Expansion has stretched its light by a factor of about 1,100, cooling it into microwaves at 2.7 kelvin: the cosmic microwave background. The sky is uniformly bright; our eyes just cannot see that color.

Darkness as Evidence

The darkness between the stars is therefore one of the oldest pieces of evidence that the universe had a beginning. A question anyone can ask while looking up connects to thermodynamics, the speed of light, stellar physics, and the Big Bang. It is a lesson in how the most ordinary observations, taken seriously, can be the deepest.

perspectives.title: Cosmological Perspective
perspectives.description: The finite age of the universe limits how many stars' light can reach us, so most sight lines end in the starless early cosmos rather than on a star.

perspectives.title: Thermodynamic Perspective
perspectives.description: Stars have finite lifetimes and the universe holds finite energy; there is not enough of either to fill space with starlight, and absorbing dust would only heat up and re-radiate.

perspectives.title: Historical Perspective
perspectives.description: Kepler used the dark sky to argue for a finite cosmos, Halley and de Chéseaux refined the puzzle, and Olbers popularized it — a debate spanning three centuries before a resolution.

perspectives.title: Literary Perspective
perspectives.description: Edgar Allan Poe's Eureka offered the essentially correct answer — light from distant stars has not yet reached us — decades before physics could support it.

perspectives.title: Observational Perspective
perspectives.description: The cosmic microwave background means every direction does end on a once-glowing surface; the sky is bright, just shifted far beyond visible wavelengths.

connections: The speed of light and lookback time
The observable universe and cosmic horizons
openQuestions: In the far future, as galaxies recede beyond our horizon, will observers lose all evidence of the Big Bang that the dark sky now provides?
How much of the extragalactic background light comes from the first generations of stars we have not yet directly observed?
Could a universe exist with an infinite past yet a dark sky, and what physics would it require?
What other everyday observations encode deep facts about cosmology that we have not yet noticed?
